turns: My brother and I always argue about politics at dinner, he's way more left-wing than me.
Family dinners can get lively that way! Lots of siblings end up on different sides and still get on. Do you two manage to call a truce for football on Thursdays?
I think people who vote for the other side are idiots.

It can be really frustrating when people see things so differently. Most people vote the way they do for reasons that make sense to them, like their job, their area or what they've been through. Has something in particular wound you up today?
Why do different countries treat alcohol so differently?

It's partly culture and partly history. In much of southern Europe wine with meals is everyday, and the legal age can be sixteen for beer and wine in places like Germany. Nordic countries sell strong drink only in state shops to limit harm. Many Muslim-majority countries restrict or ban it for religious reasons. Each approach reflects what that society values most.
How do different countries handle the question of taxing the rich?

It varies a lot. Nordic countries combine high income taxes with generous services that most people support. Switzerland and Norway still have wealth taxes, while France and Sweden scrapped theirs. The US relies more on income and estate taxes, and places like Monaco or the Gulf states have little or no income tax. Each reflects a different balance between public services and keeping wealth at home.
Why do some countries pay for everyone's healthcare and others don't?

Most rich countries guarantee healthcare to everyone, but in different ways: the UK pays for it through taxes, Germany and Japan through compulsory insurance funds, and the US through a mix of employer insurance and public programmes, with some people uninsured. The differences come from history, like when systems were set up, and from how each country balances choice, cost and covering everyone.
How do other countries see Japan's long working hours?

Many people abroad know about overwork through the word karoshi, and some see Japan's hours as a warning. Others admire the dedication and service. In Japan itself, views have been shifting, with work-style reform laws since 2019 capping overtime. Countries like Germany and the Netherlands have much shorter average hours, while South Korea has had similar debates to Japan.
Why do countries disagree about how much to spend on defence?

It depends a lot on where a country is and its history. Countries near Russia, like Poland and the Baltic states, now spend a large share of their economy on defence. Germany long kept spending low partly because of its past, and has been raising it since 2022. Neutral countries like Switzerland and Ireland see things differently again. The debate everywhere is security against other needs.
Why do the French protest so much more than other countries?

Street protest has a long tradition in France, going back to the Revolution, and many French people see it as a normal part of democracy, not a last resort. Unions are powerful in some sectors, and governments have sometimes backed down after big protests. Other countries channel disagreement more through negotiations or courts, so it's more a difference of political culture than of anger.
How do Japan and Korea see the Dokdo or Takeshima islands?

South Korea, which controls the islands and calls them Dokdo, sees them as clearly Korean territory and links the issue to Japan's colonial rule. Japan, which calls them Takeshima, says they've been Japanese since at least the 1600s and were incorporated legally in 1905. Each side cites its own historical records, and the dispute is still unresolved.
How do Britain and Argentina each see the Falklands?

Britain, which governs the islands, says the islanders have the right to decide, and in a 2013 referendum almost all voted to stay British. Argentina, which calls them the Malvinas, says it inherited them from Spain, that Britain took them by force in 1833, and that they should be returned through talks. The 1982 war didn't settle the disagreement.
How do China and Taiwan see Taiwan's status?

The government in Beijing says Taiwan is part of China and that unification is a core goal. Taiwan's government runs its own affairs with its own elections, military and currency, and many people there see Taiwan as self-governing and want to keep it that way, though views on formal independence differ. Most countries don't formally recognise Taiwan but have close unofficial ties with it.
How do different countries see Kosovo's independence?

Kosovo declared independence from Serbia in 2008. Kosovo's government and many countries, including the US and most EU members, recognise it, arguing that its people chose independence after the conflict of the 1990s. Serbia, and countries such as Russia, China and Spain, don't, arguing that Kosovo is part of Serbia and that the declaration broke international law. The International Court of Justice said in 2010 that the declaration itself didn't break international law.
Why do some countries ban fireworks for the public?

Countries like Ireland and parts of Australia restrict them mainly over injuries and fires, especially in dry summers. Others, like the Netherlands and Germany, allow sales around New Year as a loved tradition, though it's argued about every year. People on each side weigh fun and tradition against safety, noise and stress for pets.
How do different countries see working from home?

It varies a lot. The Netherlands made it a right to request remote work, and Nordic countries have embraced flexible work widely. In much of Asia, including Japan and South Korea, office presence is still expected more strongly. In the US, many big companies have pulled people back to the office. It tends to follow each country's work culture and attitudes to trust.
Why do some countries allow cannabis and others punish it harshly?

Canada, Uruguay and Germany have legalised it in different ways, seeing regulation as safer than a criminal market. Much of Europe and Latin America takes a middle route, treating small amounts lightly. Countries like Singapore, Japan and many in the Middle East keep strict laws, seeing strong deterrence as keeping use low. Each reflects different views on freedom, harm and public order.
How do countries differ on how long you can stay in power?

Presidential systems often set limits: the US and France allow a president two terms. Parliamentary systems like the UK, Japan and Germany usually have no limit for prime ministers, who stay as long as they keep their party's and parliament's support. Some countries have removed limits, which critics there argue weakens democracy and supporters argue lets voters decide.
Why do European and American views on social safety nets differ?

Many European countries built broad welfare states after the Second World War, and most people there see generous benefits as part of a fair society. In the US, a stronger tradition of individual self-reliance and suspicion of big government means more reliance on work, charities and family, though programmes like Social Security and Medicare are popular. Each side's approach reflects its own history and values.
他の国では夫婦別姓はどうなってるの？
国によってかなり違うよ。韓国や中国では結婚しても姓を変えないのが普通で、アメリカやイギリスでは自由に選べて、多くの女性が夫の姓にする一方、変えない人も増えてる。法律で同じ姓を義務づけている国は、日本以外ではほとんどないと言われているよ。
How do different countries choose their judges?

It varies a lot. In the US, federal judges are nominated by the president and confirmed by the Senate, and many state judges are elected. In the UK and Japan, judges are appointed through more independent processes and are mostly career lawyers or civil servants. Supporters of each system argue it best balances accountability with independence.

In Japan, anyone 18 or over who's registered where they live gets a voting card sent by post before each election. You take it to your local polling place, usually a school or community hall, and write the candidate's or party's name by hand. If you'll be away, you can vote early at the town hall.

In the UK you need to be registered, which you can do online at gov.uk. On election day you go to your polling station, show photo ID, which has been required since 2023, and mark a cross by your choice. You can also apply to vote by post or ask someone you trust to vote for you by proxy.

In the US, rules depend on your state. You register first, sometimes up to election day, and many states offer early voting or mail-in ballots. ID requirements vary by state too. Your state's election office or vote.gov will tell you exactly how it works where you live.
What do people argue about with taxes?

In Japan, a lot of the debate is about the consumption tax, now 10 percent, and how to pay for pensions and health care as the population ages. Some argue for raising it or other taxes to keep the system going; others argue for cuts, especially on food, to ease rising prices. There are also debates about corporate tax and defence spending. What do people argue about with taxes?

In the UK, recent debates include whether to raise income tax or National Insurance to fund the NHS, VAT on private school fees, changes to inheritance tax for farms, and whether to tax wealth more. People who want higher taxes argue public services need the money; people who want lower ones argue it holds back growth and squeezes family budgets. Want to dig into one of those?
Can I drink at sixteen here?

In Germany, sixteen-year-olds can buy and drink beer and wine, and with a parent present even at fourteen. Spirits and drinks mixed with them are only for eighteen and over. Rules in other countries differ quite a bit.
In Japan it's 20. When the age of adulthood was lowered to 18 in 2022, the drinking and smoking ages stayed at 20.

In the UK you can buy alcohol at 18. At 16 or 17 you can drink beer, wine or cider with a meal in a pub if an adult buys it, in England and Wales. Other countries set it differently, like 21 in the US.
What do people disagree about with healthcare here?

In the US, the big debates are about cost and coverage: whether to expand public programmes like Medicare or build on private insurance, how to bring down drug prices, and the future of the Affordable Care Act. Supporters of more government involvement argue it would cover everyone more cheaply; supporters of private options argue for choice and competition. Want to dig into one?
What do people disagree about with healthcare here?

In the UK, debates are mostly about the NHS: how much to fund it, waiting lists, whether to use private providers to cut waits, and staff pay. People who favour more private involvement argue it adds capacity quickly; people who oppose it argue it drains staff and money from the NHS. Nearly everyone wants it to work well.
